messages.author: a3528cfc1d2614c7
messages.subject: multilevel modeling w/inlabru
parts:
Hello,

I was drawn to check out "inlabru" because it seems like it would be of use for the bird count data I work with. I have previously published a chapter of my dissertation which used R-INLA for the North American Breeding Bird Survey data set: https://pubs.er.usgs.gov/publication/70179080

For my current analysis, I am hoping to assess guild-level response but allowing slope to vary by species, to see the nuance in species' response while still assessing the response of the guild. So for example, my data frame looks like...

Survey_Route Year    Species                        Guild                            Count CovariateX
001                   1986  Rusty blackbird            short-distance migrant  5        0.9
001                   1987  Rusty blackbird            short-distance migrant  7        0.5
001                   1987  Blackburnian warbler   long-distance migrant   2        0.5
002                   1986  Blackburnian warbler   long-distance migrant   8        0.2

So for this hypothetical, I want to estimate the coefficient of Co-variate X for each guild, but within the model, I also want to assess how each species' response deviates from the guild response.

I had an R-INLA formulation to do this like...
f(species, CovariateX, model = 'iid')

I'm not sure how to translate this for inlabru, though.

I found an example with spatial modeling...

cmp = lethal ~ Intercept+
   myspde(map = coordinates,
   group = Year,
   ngroup = nyear,
   model = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, alpha=1.5, prior.range=c(0.1,0.01), prior.sigma=c(1,0.01)),
   mesh = mesh,
   control.group=list(model="ar1"))

I'm wondering if that's how the formulation would change, but also with the note that as far as I can understand how to apply this (which might be wrong) I have several other "grouping factors," such as year. Also, my previous models weren't spatially explicit but I'm thinking about moving to that framework to deal with auto-correlation. So, any advice on formulation of multilevel models in inlabru is much appreciated!

Thanks,
Jess

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] multilevel modeling w/inlabru
parts:
Hi,
we haven't set up a separate mailing list for inlabru yet, but I try
to respond to inlabru specific questions that appear here.

Factors still have shaky support, but if you first convert them to
indices (from 1 to #levels) the inla() and bru() models below are
equivalent:

data <- data.frame(mycov = rnorm(20), myfactor=c(1:10, 1:10))
data$y <- data$mycov * rnorm(10)[data$myfactor] + rnorm(20, sd = 0.01)

res <- inla(formula = y ~ -1 + f(myfactor, mycov, model="iid"), data=data)

res2 <- bru(~ -1 + eff(map=myfactor, model="iid", n=10), data=data,
like("gaussian", formula = y ~ mycov * eff))

summary(res)
INLA:::summary.inla(res2)

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] multilevel modeling w/inlabru
parts:
That would be equivalent to
(CovA + CovB) * eff
which is probably not what you want?
There are two possible situation, depending on if you want the same variance for the effects or not. If you want one precision parameter for each of them, then just define two effects, effA and effB, and use them as
CovA*effA + CovB*effB

For a common precision, I’m not actually sure how to do it in a simple way in inlabru; in raw INLA one can use the “copy” feature with fixed scaling, or construct a model with inla.stack(), but I’d need to see a concrete use case to figure it out for inlabru (I suspect it would require a new feature in the interface, or a more complex construction in the formula).

Finn

parts:
Hi Finn,

Thanks again, you're right! I went with one precision parameter for each so I instead formulated as...

cmp <- abundance ~ yearfix + extra(map = rteobs, model = "iid", n=n_obs) + firstyear + extra2(map = Year, model = "iid", n=n_yr) + extra3(map = AOU, model = "iid", n=n_spp) + SPI + STI + MN + 
             effA(map=AOU, model="iid", n=n_spp) + effB(map=AOU, model="iid", n=n_spp) + effC(map=AOU, model="iid", n=n_spp)
candidate = abundance ~ yearfix + extra + firstyear + extra2 + SPI*STI + STI*effA + SPI*effB + extra3  
fitted = bru(cmp, data=weatherdata, like("gpoisson", formula = candidate), control.compute = list(waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, config=TRUE), verbose=FALSE)

Let me know if that looks right. Is gpoisson supported in inlabru? I'm getting the following error, which I'm assuming is internal to inlabru because I don't have anything named this in my script:
Error in lh$data : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors 

I'm not sure if this matters but FYI I'm running my script on a Linux HPC system.
Thanks,
Jess

parts:
Hi,
what inlabru and INLA versions do you have?
The inlabru development version has a number of bug fixes that are not yet in the realeased/stable versions.
See inlabru.org for information about installing it from github.

What’s the output from
traceback()
after the error?

All likelihoods in INLA can in principle be used in inlabru; some that require extra input might not work fully yet though, and we haven’t extensively tested them. (E.g., I believe the CRAN version only handles Ntrials=1 for binomial likelihoods; not sure about the main development branch version on that point).

Finn

On Tue, Jun 19, 2018 at 2:19 PM Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
That would be equivalent to
(CovA + CovB) * eff
which is probably not what you want?
There are two possible situation, depending on if you want the same variance for the effects or not. If you want one precision parameter for each of them, then just define two effects, effA and effB, and use them as
CovA*effA + CovB*effB

For a common precision, I’m not actually sure how to do it in a simple way in inlabru; in raw INLA one can use the “copy” feature with fixed scaling, or construct a model with inla.stack(), but I’d need to see a concrete use case to figure it out for inlabru (I suspect it would require a new feature in the interface, or a more complex construction in the formula).


Finn

On Tue, Jun 19, 2018 at 5:21 AM Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi,
we haven't set up a separate mailing list for inlabru yet, but I try
to respond to inlabru specific questions that appear here.

Factors still have shaky support, but if you first convert them to
indices (from 1 to #levels) the inla() and bru() models below are
equivalent:

data <- data.frame(mycov = rnorm(20), myfactor=c(1:10, 1:10))
data$y <- data$mycov * rnorm(10)[data$myfactor] + rnorm(20, sd = 0.01)

res <- inla(formula = y ~ -1 + f(myfactor, mycov, model="iid"), data=data)

res2 <- bru(~ -1 + eff(map=myfactor, model="iid", n=10), data=data,
     like("gaussian", formula = y ~ mycov * eff))

summary(res)
INLA:::summary.inla(res2)

Finn

I'm debugging some further inlabru/inla issues off-list, but the
specific error was this:
In the inlabru::bru() call, control.compute and verbose need to be
wrapped in the options parameter list, which is mostly passed on to
inla().
